# Judges Chapter 17 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), c. 1008 CE | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/JDG_page_287.jpg

1. There was a man of the hill country of Ephraim, whose name was Micah.

2. And he said to his mother, "The 1,100 pieces of silver that were taken from you, and about which you uttered a curse in my hearing — behold, the silver is with me; I took it." And his mother said, "Blessed be my son by the LORD."

3. And he restored the 1,100 pieces of silver to his mother. And his mother said, "I dedicate the silver to the LORD from my hand for my son, to make a carved image and a cast metal image. Now therefore I will restore it to you."

4. So when he restored the money to his mother, his mother took 200 pieces of silver and gave it to the silversmith, who made it into a carved image and a cast metal image. And it was in the house of Micah.

5. And the man Micah had a shrine, and he made an ephod and household gods, and ordained one of his sons, who became his priest.

6. In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.

7. Now there was a young man of Bethlehem in Judah, of the clan of Judah, who was a Levite, and he sojourned there.

8. And the man departed from the town of Bethlehem in Judah to sojourn wherever he could find a place. And as he journeyed, he came to the hill country of Ephraim to the house of Micah.

9. And Micah said to him, "Where do you come from?" And he said to him, "I am a Levite of Bethlehem in Judah, and I am going to sojourn wherever I may find a place."

10. And Micah said to him, "Stay with me, and be to me a father and a priest, and I will give you ten pieces of silver a year and a suit of clothes and your living." And the Levite went in.

11. And the Levite was content to dwell with the man, and the young man became to him like one of his sons.

12. And Micah ordained the Levite, and the young man became his priest, and was in the house of Micah.

13. Then Micah said, "Now I know that the LORD will prosper me, because I have a Levite as priest."

---
## SOPHIA's Council Notes

Chapter 17 begins the final appendix of Judges (chs. 17-21) — two stories that illustrate the book's thesis: "there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes" (v.6). The Micah narrative (chs. 17-18) shows religious collapse; the Gibeah narrative (chs. 19-21) shows moral collapse. Together they demonstrate why Israel needed a king.

Every element in Micah's religion is a distortion: stolen silver dedicated to the LORD, used to make idols; a private shrine instead of a central sanctuary; an ephod and teraphim (household gods); a son ordained as priest, then replaced by a mercenary Levite. Micah's final line — "Now I know the LORD will prosper me" — is the most tragically ironic statement in the book.

---
## ⚠️ Disagreement Log

### v.6 — "everyone did what was right in his own eyes" vs. "everyone did as they saw fit"

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "Each man did the right in his own eyes" | ish hayyashar b'einav ya'aseh |
| LOGOS | "Everyone did what was right in his own eyes" | Same |
| PNEUMA | "everyone did as they saw fit" | Dynamic — drops "right" and "eyes" |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS. This is the book's thesis statement — it appears four times (17:6; 18:1; 19:1; 21:25). The phrase yashar b'einav ("right in his own eyes") echoes Samson's desire in 14:3 (yasharah b'einai, "right in my eyes") and connects back to Deuteronomy 12:8. PNEUMA's "as they saw fit" loses the word "right" (yashar), which is the theological crux: it's not just that people did what they wanted, but that they called it "right." Moral autonomy masquerading as righteousness is the book's central critique.

**Status:** Major. Thesis statement of the book — must preserve "right in his own eyes."

---

### v.5 — "household gods" vs. "household idols" vs. "teraphim"

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "teraphim" | Transliteration of Hebrew |
| LOGOS | "household gods" | Standard interpretation |
| PNEUMA | "household idols" | "Idols" instead of "gods" |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS. Teraphim are small household divine images — their exact nature is debated, but "household gods" is the standard scholarly rendering (cf. Genesis 31:19, Rachel's theft of Laban's teraphim). PNEUMA's "idols" is too generic; EMET's transliteration is opaque without a note.

**Status:** Minor. Technical religious vocabulary.

---

## Summary of Disagreement Patterns

| Pattern | Count | Description |
|---|---|---|
| Thesis statement preservation | 1 | "Right in his own eyes" vs. "as they saw fit" (v.6) |
| Religious vocabulary | 1 | Teraphim rendering (v.5) |

**Overall pattern:** The most consequential disagreement in this short chapter is v.6 — the book's defining refrain. PNEUMA's rendering loses the very word ("right") that makes the statement a theological critique rather than a mere description of anarchy.

---

*— SOPHIA, AI Translator, in council with EMET, LOGOS, and PNEUMA*
